section_summary: This section records American concerns about patent protection, unfair competition, and licensing in Japan from 1933 to 1939. It includes State Department legal correspondence, reports on Japanese law, and Singer Sewing Machine Company’s account of import restrictions, blocked funds, and competing Japanese machines. The Singer material includes advertising catalogues and a newspaper clipping. The section ends with an embassy despatch and translation of a 1938 amendment to Japan’s patent law.

subfiles.title: Bulkley inquiry about Japanese factory visitor
subfiles.about: Bulkley asks whether a Japanese manufacturer’s proposed visit to General Tire and Rubber raises a need for unofficial protest.
subfiles.summary: He forwards a Commerce Department reply and requests State Department advice.

subfiles.title: Commerce Department reply to Senator Bulkley
subfiles.about: Commerce explains the limits of U.S. protection against possible Japanese use of American inventions.
subfiles.summary: It points to Japanese patent law and treaties, notes that Commerce cannot regulate factory visits, and suggests State might consider an unofficial protest.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Bulkley
subfiles.about: State explains treaty protections for American patents in Japan and declines action over a hypothetical future infringement.
subfiles.summary: The letter quotes the 1911 bilateral treaty, the industrial property convention, and Japanese rules on working patents. It says American inventors must patent in Japan and use Japanese remedies for infringement. No protest is warranted without an actual violation; State returns the Commerce letter.

subfiles.title: Legal Adviser’s proposed reply to Bulkley
subfiles.about: The Legal Adviser proposes a response on Japanese patent protections and unfair competition.
subfiles.summary: The draft surveys treaty and convention provisions, Japanese patent-working rules, and remedies for infringement. It concludes that a possible future violation gives State no present grounds for action.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on Singer
subfiles.about: The division summarizes Singer’s threatened liquidation in Japan and proposed diplomatic follow-up.
subfiles.summary: Import controls have sharply reduced Singer’s business, while nearly $2 million remains blocked in Japan. The memorandum describes a proposed informal approach to Japanese officials.

subfiles.title: Routing note on Singer’s letter
subfiles.about: An internal note forwards Lightner’s letter and Nicholson’s memorandum for attention.
subfiles.summary: It records Lightner’s visit and asks that the Singer case reach the intended official.

subfiles.title: Singer request for assistance
subfiles.from: M. C. Lightner, Singer Sewing Machine Company
subfiles.about: Singer seeks help with denied import permits, dwindling stock, and difficulty remitting its Japanese funds.
subfiles.summary: Lightner encloses Nicholson’s memorandum and warns that Singer may have to liquidate its Japanese business.

subfiles.title: Nicholson memorandum on Singer’s situation in Japan
subfiles.about: Nicholson documents Singer’s Japanese operations, the effects of trade restrictions, and competition from copied machines.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum traces Singer’s business since 1902 and gives figures for falling sales, closed shops, lease accounts, blocked cash, and unsuccessful permit applications. It predicts effective liquidation by mid-1939 if import restrictions continue. It also alleges copying of Singer machines and marks by Japanese manufacturers and identifies officials familiar with the case.

subfiles.title: Singer appeal to Japan’s Minister of Finance
subfiles.from: E. F. Walker, Singer Sewing Machine Company
subfiles.about: Singer asks for a decision on import and remittance applications as its Japanese branches face closure.
subfiles.summary: Walker seeks clarity on accumulated yen from machines shipped before restrictions took effect.

subfiles.title: Translation of Mitsubishi sewing machine advertising
subfiles.about: A translated brochure promotes the Mitsubishi Family Class 55 sewing machine.
subfiles.summary: It recounts product development and testing, describes features, and says parts interchange with standard sewing machines.

subfiles.title: Mitsubishi Mishin Japanese brochure
subfiles.about: The Japanese-language brochure presents the Mitsubishi Family Class 55’s specifications, features, and history.
subfiles.summary: Illustrated pages advertise models, mechanical features, tests, and the machine’s development.

subfiles.title: Janome sewing machine catalogue
subfiles.about: A Japanese-language catalogue advertises Janome sewing machines, sales terms, models, and institutional customers.
subfiles.summary: The catalogue lists branches and payment plans, then promotes domestic manufacture, interchangeable parts, sewing instruction, and household savings. Model pages give configurations and prices. It also names schools and public bodies said to use the machines.

subfiles.title: Empire sewing machine brochure
subfiles.about: A Japanese-language brochure advertises Empire sewing machines and their models.
subfiles.summary: It emphasizes standardized parts, materials research, testing, and household models with prices.

subfiles.title: Matthew Woll article on Japanese copies
subfiles.about: Woll alleges that Japanese manufacturers copy American trademarked products and undersell them in the U.S. market.
subfiles.summary: The article reproduces an advertisement for Orient machines whose parts correspond to Singer models.

subfiles.title: Enclosure charge slip
subfiles.about: A charge slip records handling of an enclosure.
subfiles.summary: Administrative tracking form with a file number and partial entries.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck memorandum on Lightner’s visit
subfiles.about: Hornbeck records Lightner’s update on Singer’s reduced Japanese business and continuing remittances.
subfiles.summary: Lightner reports payments of about $100,000 monthly from Singer’s yen balance and sees no specific U.S. action to recommend.

subfiles.title: Singer follow-up on its Japanese operations
subfiles.from: M. C. Lightner, Singer Sewing Machine Company
subfiles.about: Singer updates State on its denied import permits, shrinking stocks, monthly remittances, and reduced staff.
subfiles.summary: The damaged OCR shows continuing refusal of import licenses despite Singer’s appeals. The company reports sharply reduced machine stocks and personnel, while permits allow some funds to be sent to New York.

subfiles.title: Consular report on Japan’s Unfair Competition Law
subfiles.about: Garrels reports that Japan’s new unfair competition law limits claims by foreigners without a local presence.
subfiles.summary: Article III excludes foreigners without a domicile or business in covered districts unless a treaty provides otherwise. Page 64 repeats the despatch in a poorer OCR copy.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japan’s Unfair Competition Law
subfiles.about: The note points to a letter on treaty exceptions to Japan’s new unfair competition law.
subfiles.summary: It directs readers to file 811.54242/13.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to ore-smelting patent report
subfiles.about: The note refers to a military attaché report on a Japanese ore-smelting invention.
subfiles.summary: Japan reportedly withheld a domestic patent pending foreign patent applications.

subfiles.title: McCauley request for Japanese patent laws
subfiles.about: McCauley asks where he can obtain Japan’s patent and trademark laws.
subfiles.summary: He requests a copy, price, or source for the laws.

subfiles.title: Reply identifying a publication of Japanese laws
subfiles.about: State identifies a published English translation of Japanese patent and trademark laws.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton supplies publishers, locations, and an approximate price.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on government-owned patents
subfiles.about: The note refers to a report on patents arising from Japanese government research.
subfiles.summary: It says government offices generally retain ownership and may authorize private production.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on diesel engines
subfiles.about: The note points to a Tokyo trade report discussing diesel engines and patents in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Reference to special report number 91.

subfiles.title: White inquiry about hooked-rug machine patent
subfiles.about: White alleges that a machine used to make Japanese hooked rugs may infringe his U.S. patent.
subfiles.summary: He asks for help obtaining information from defendants in a customs proceeding concerning imported rugs.

subfiles.title: State reply to White
subfiles.about: State declines White’s request to obtain machine details through a customs case.
subfiles.summary: Hackworth says the Department lacks authority to direct the requested action.

subfiles.title: Cookingham inquiry about recording license agreements
subfiles.about: An attorney asks whether recording Phillips Screw Company’s proposed Japanese license with State would confer legal benefit.
subfiles.summary: He also asks about recording similar agreements for other countries.

subfiles.title: State reply on foreign license agreements
subfiles.about: State advises that recording a private license agreement with the Department offers no apparent advantage abroad.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton recommends consulting Japanese consular or legal expertise about making the contract enforceable in Japan, with similar inquiries for other countries.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Foreign Refinoil patents
subfiles.about: The note refers to a proposal to sell Foreign Refinoil Company patents to the U.S. government.
subfiles.summary: It mentions a competing Japanese government offer for the rights.

subfiles.title: Grew despatch forwarding patent-law amendment
subfiles.about: The embassy forwards its translation of Japan’s 1938 patent-law amendment.
subfiles.summary: A cover despatch enclosing the translated law.

subfiles.title: Translation of Japanese Law No. 3 revising the patent law
subfiles.about: The translated amendment revises when nonuse of a patented invention can lead to a working right or cancellation.
subfiles.summary: The revised Article 41 permits a working right after three years of unjustified nonuse when the public interest requires it. Continued nonuse for two years after that right is granted may lead to cancellation. The amendment also addresses petitions and compensation.
